result:
**Bottom line:** Read it if you're building a SKILL.md linter or quality rubric — the 26-smell catalog and the judge prompt design are directly reusable. Skip the full text if you want evidence that any of this actually improves agent behavior; the paper doesn't test that.

**What it is:** First empirical study treating SKILL.md as a software artifact. Three deliverables: (1) a component taxonomy (13 higher-level / 44 lower-level sections) derived from qualitative coding of 238 marketplace skills; (2) 26 "skill smells" produced by inverting 26 community best practices harvested from a multivocal literature review of 29 web sources; (3) SSD, an automated detector — 5 smells caught statically, 21 via an LLM judge (quantized Qwen3.6-27B, per-smell definition plus one positive and one negative example, binary output). Weighted F1 0.78 against 53 hand-labeled files.

**Headline findings:** >99% of skills carry at least one smell, averaging 10.5 each; exactly one of 238 files is clean. Rationalization Loophole (nothing discourages the agent from skipping required steps) hits 94%. Section usage is thin beyond the basics — Task 74%, Introduction 64%, References 57%, then a steep drop-off. Only 7 of 13 top-level components have any community guidance at all. Smells accumulate over a skill's lifetime and rarely get removed.

**The load-bearing caveat:** the "best practices" are folklore — top-50 web search results, filtered to 29, conflicts resolved by majority vote. Nothing establishes that a smell degrades agent performance. Prevalence numbers may just describe what community advice happens to be unpopular. Add a sample skewed toward popular public marketplace skills and a detector validated on 53 files with one quantized open model, and treat every number as indicative rather than settled.

**What's worth extracting** (roughly a 20-minute skim of the smell catalog and detector section, if that's your interest):
- The static/judge split is well-drawn — length caps, backslash paths, and XML-in-frontmatter are cheap script checks; everything else needs a judge.
- The judge prompt framing (definition + one positive + one negative example + binary answer) is copyable as-is.
- The `[what it does] + [when to use] + [keywords]` description rule works as a trigger-quality check.
- F1 0.78 is a reasonable bar to beat, provided you measure the same way on your own fixtures.

**Skip if:** you want causal evidence, you're targeting private or enterprise skills rather than marketplace ones, or you only need the catalog — in which case the smell list above is essentially the paper's payload.
